prompt_free_text:
This paper introduces X-Topic, a multilingual multi-label topic classification dataset for X/Twitter posts in English, Spanish, Japanese, and Greek, and benchmarks a range of fine-tuned multilingual encoders and prompted LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, monolingual, cross-lingual, and multilingual settings. Overall, I find the paper timely, practically useful, and likely to be valuable to the community as a dataset-and-benchmark contribution. The topic taxonomy is broader than many prior social media resources, the multilingual angle is meaningful, and the empirical study is fairly extensive. The paper’s main strengths are the release of a new annotated resource, the comparison across several realistic transfer settings, and the clear empirical takeaway that domain-specific multilingual encoders remain highly competitive relative to much larger prompted LLMs for this task.

At the same time, I have several concerns about dataset construction choices, evaluation design, and the interpretation of some conclusions. These issues do not negate the usefulness of the resource, but they do affect how strongly I would trust some of the claims. In particular, the dataset is quite small per language, the annotation agreement is modest, the label aggregation rule is permissive, and some comparisons confound language transfer with training set size and temporal shift. I therefore view the paper as a solid resource paper with interesting analysis, but not yet a fully definitive study of multilingual topic classification.

The contribution is clear. A multilingual social-media topic dataset with 19 labels and multi-label annotations is indeed a gap in current resources. The inclusion of typologically diverse languages is a plus, especially Japanese and Greek, and the paper does a good job motivating why social media topic classification differs from standard news classification. The benchmark settings are also well chosen from an application perspective: zero-shot and few-shot for low-resource deployment, cross-lingual transfer from English, monolingual fine-tuning with limited target data, and multilingual training across all languages. This breadth makes the paper more useful than a simple dataset release.

The dataset collection methodology is sensible in spirit but raises some representativeness questions. The authors emphasize that unlike the original TweetTopic, they do not use keyword filtering and instead sample tweets more broadly, which is a good design choice if the goal is realism. However, the later weighted sampling by retweet count and follower count introduces a different bias toward popular or high-visibility content. This may improve readability or annotation efficiency, but it also shifts the distribution away from “real” random X content and toward more socially amplified posts. Since the paper explicitly contrasts itself with keyword-based collection as being closer to the real distribution, this popularity-weighted sampling should be discussed more carefully as a source of bias. It would help to quantify how much the sampled set differs from the pre-sampled pool in topic distribution, user type, or lexical properties.

The preprocessing pipeline also deserves more scrutiny. Removing tweets with URLs, many emojis, many mentions, incomplete sentences, “abusing words,” and near-duplicates likely improves annotation quality, but it may systematically exclude important genres of social media discourse. For topic classification on X, URLs and mentions are often central signals, especially for news, business, politics, fandom, and activism. Similarly, emoji-heavy posts are common in entertainment and daily-life categories. The resulting benchmark may therefore be cleaner but less representative of the platform. This is not necessarily wrong, but the paper should frame X-Topic as a curated subset of X rather than a direct sample of platform content. An ablation or descriptive comparison before and after filtering would strengthen the paper substantially.

The annotation setup is mostly standard and reasonably documented, but the label aggregation rule is debatable. Assigning a label when at least two of five annotators agree is intentionally permissive and does create a challenging multi-label benchmark. However, it also risks inflating label cardinality and introducing noisy positives, especially for semantically adjacent categories such as diaries & daily life, relationships, family, arts & culture, and other hobbies. The reported average of 1.8 topics per tweet is relatively high, and the low Krippendorff alpha values around 0.21–0.26 suggest substantial ambiguity. The authors argue that these agreement levels are comparable to other difficult multi-label tasks, which is fair, but topic classification may be less inherently subjective than emotion annotation, so the comparison is not entirely reassuring. Releasing all raw annotations is excellent, but the paper would be stronger if it included sensitivity analyses under alternative aggregation rules, such as majority vote, confidence-weighted labels, or at least reporting performance on a high-agreement subset. That would help disentangle task difficulty from annotation noise.

Relatedly, the agreement metrics are somewhat hard to interpret without more detail on how alpha is computed for the multi-label setting. Multi-label reliability can vary substantially depending on whether one computes agreement per label, per instance-label matrix, or over label sets. The paper should specify this more precisely. It would also be useful to report per-topic agreement or prevalence-adjusted agreement, since some labels are likely much more ambiguous than others. Given that the benchmark’s value depends heavily on annotation quality, this deserves more space.

The experimental section is broad and generally well executed, but some comparisons are not fully controlled. The most notable issue is the interpretation of cross-lingual versus monolingual performance. The paper highlights that models trained on English TweetTopic outperform monolingual models trained on the target-language subset, and presents this as evidence of strong cross-lingual transfer. While that is partly true, the comparison is heavily confounded by training size: 11,267 English examples versus only 800 target-language training examples per fold. The authors acknowledge this, but the framing still overstates the cross-lingual conclusion. A more convincing analysis would subsample TweetTopic to match the target-language training size, or plot performance as a function of training set size for both source and target data. Without that, the result mainly shows that more labeled data in a related domain can beat less labeled data in the target language.

A similar issue appears in the multilingual versus monolingual comparison. The multilingual gains are interesting and plausible, especially for lower-resource languages, but again they may largely reflect increased total training volume rather than multilingual synergy per se. This does not invalidate the result, but the paper should be more careful in attributing the gains. A controlled experiment with equalized total numbers of training instances would help establish whether multilinguality itself is beneficial beyond simple data scaling.

The benchmark against LLMs is useful, but the comparison is somewhat uneven. Prompted GPT-4o performs surprisingly strongly, especially in macro-F1, and the paper’s conclusion that fine-tuned encoders remain competitive is well supported. However, the LLM evaluation depends heavily on prompt design, output parsing, label verbalization, and decoding settings, none of which are discussed in enough detail in the main paper. Since few-shot prompting can be highly sensitive to example selection and label descriptions, the fairness and reproducibility of this comparison are limited. Also, comparing API-based proprietary models to fine-tuned open encoders is practically relevant, but the paper should be explicit that this is not a like-for-like scientific comparison in terms of controllability or reproducibility. Cost and latency comparisons would also make the practical takeaway much stronger.

The evaluation metric choice is appropriate overall. Macro-F1 is the right primary metric for imbalanced multi-label classification, and reporting micro-F1 is helpful. Still, the paper would benefit from additional metrics tailored to multi-label tasks, such as exact match, subset accuracy, Hamming loss, label ranking average precision, or example-based F1. Because some models appear to differ mainly in label cardinality calibration, example-based metrics could reveal important behavior hidden by macro/micro aggregation. The discussion around chat-gpt predicting more labels per tweet is insightful; this suggests that thresholding or calibration may matter a lot. For fine-tuned models, it is not clear how decision thresholds are chosen for each label. If a fixed threshold of 0.5 is used, that may be suboptimal under severe imbalance. Threshold tuning on validation data could materially change the results and should be described.

The results themselves are interesting. The strongest empirical takeaway is that domain-adapted multilingual encoders, especially XLM-T large, perform very well and often better than generic XLM-R, confirming the importance of social-media pretraining. This is a valuable result. The multilingual training gains are also useful, and the fact that GPT-4o is competitive in few-shot mode but not uniformly dominant is noteworthy. I also appreciated the error analysis pointing to difficult labels such as Other Hobbies and Arts & Culture. These categories seem semantically diffuse and likely deserve either refinement or hierarchical treatment in future work.

That said, some of the interpretation could be sharpened. For example, the paper states that recent LLMs underperform compared to “more efficient but fully-trained multilingual masked language models,” but Table 3 shows GPT-4o few-shot is actually competitive with or better than several fine-tuned settings, and even best on Greek macro-F1. The more precise conclusion is that fine-tuned domain-specific encoders remain highly competitive and often superior when sufficient labeled data is available, not that LLMs broadly underperform. The distinction matters.

The paper would also benefit from stronger statistical reporting. Table 3 mentions statistically significant differences, but the test used, the unit of analysis, and the correction for multiple comparisons are not described here. With 5-fold cross-validation on only 1,000 examples per language, variance could be substantial. Reporting mean and standard deviation across folds, or confidence intervals, would make the conclusions more credible. This is especially important when differences are only 1–2 F1 points.

Another concern is the temporal and platform framing. The paper refers to “X” but the data period is 2021–2022, overlapping the Twitter era. This is mostly cosmetic, but the paper should be consistent about whether it studies Twitter/X historically or current X. More importantly, the cross-lingual TweetTopic-to-X-Topic transfer includes temporal shift as well as collection-method shift, which complicates interpretation. Since TweetTopic used trending keywords and X-Topic uses broad sampling, the source-target mismatch is not only language and time but also sampling strategy. This should be emphasized more clearly.

There are also some presentation issues. The paper contains a noticeable number of typos and grammatical errors, and Table 3 is difficult to parse in its current formatting. Some model names are inconsistently written, and there are a few awkward or inaccurate descriptions, such as calling ChatGPT-3.5 an encoder/decoder model with approximately 175B parameters. The paper would benefit from careful proofreading and clearer table design. These are not fatal issues, but they do affect readability.

I have several concrete suggestions that would significantly strengthen the paper. First, add controlled analyses that disentangle transfer effects from training size, ideally by subsampling TweetTopic and multilingual training data to matched sizes. Second, report more annotation details: per-topic agreement, exact alpha computation, and sensitivity to alternative label aggregation rules. Third, provide more transparency on thresholding, prompt design, output normalization, and statistical testing. Fourth, include a short bias/representativeness analysis of the filtering and popularity-weighted sampling pipeline. Fifth, if feasible, add a high-agreement subset evaluation or soft-label evaluation to assess robustness to annotation noise. Finally, consider discussing whether some labels should be merged, hierarchically organized, or redefined, especially the broad “Other Hobbies” category.

In terms of significance, I think the dataset itself is the main contribution and is likely to be useful. Four languages and 4,000 annotated tweets is not large, but for multi-label social media topic classification it is still a meaningful resource, especially with open release and accompanying models. The empirical findings are mostly confirmatory rather than groundbreaking, but they are still valuable because they are grounded in a new benchmark. I would be more enthusiastic if the paper did more to isolate causal factors behind the observed gains and more rigorously addressed annotation noise.

My overall assessment is positive but somewhat tempered. This is a worthwhile benchmark paper with practical value, a sensible experimental scope, and useful findings about multilingual and domain-specific modeling for social media topic classification. Its main weaknesses are limited dataset scale, modest annotation reliability, and several confounds in the comparative analysis. If accepted, I would encourage the authors to revise the framing of their claims and improve methodological transparency.

I would lean toward acceptance if the venue values dataset and benchmark contributions, though not as a top-tier empirical modeling paper. The resource is useful and the experiments are broad, but the paper should be careful not to overclaim beyond what the current evidence supports.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper introduces X-Topic, a multilingual multi-label tweet topic classification dataset covering English, Spanish, Japanese, and Greek, with 1,000 annotated tweets per language and a 19-topic taxonomy inherited from prior English-only work. The paper also provides an empirical benchmark across zero-shot, few-shot, monolingual, cross-lingual, and multilingual settings using both fine-tuned multilingual encoders and prompted LLMs. The main findings are that multilingual and cross-lingual supervised models, especially tweet-domain-specific encoders such as XLM-T, outperform monolingual low-resource training and generally outperform few-shot LLMs on average, although GPT-4o is competitive in some settings.
strengths: The paper addresses a real resource gap by releasing a multilingual social-media topic classification benchmark with four typologically diverse languages, including a relatively underrepresented language (Greek).
The dataset construction process is described in reasonable detail, including collection period, preprocessing, annotation setup, and agreement statistics.

The benchmark is broad and practically useful: it compares zero-shot, few-shot, monolingual, cross-lingual, and multilingual training regimes, which gives the paper value beyond simple dataset release.

The empirical comparison includes both generic multilingual models and tweet-specialized encoders, yielding a useful conclusion that domain-specific pretraining matters substantially for social-media topic classification.
The paper reports both macro-F1 and micro-F1, which is appropriate for imbalanced multi-label classification.
The release of data and trained models increases reproducibility and likely community impact.
weaknesses: The dataset is quite small for a benchmark intended to support multilingual analysis: only 1,000 tweets per language, with substantial class imbalance and low agreement, limits the strength of downstream conclusions.

The annotation aggregation rule of assigning a label when only 2 of 5 annotators agree is weak and likely introduces substantial label noise, especially given the already low Krippendorff alpha values (0.21-0.26).

The sampling procedure is biased toward tweets with higher retweet counts and higher-follower users, which undermines the claim of approximating the real distribution of X content and may distort topic prevalence and style.

Several central claims are confounded by training-set size differences, especially the conclusion that cross-lingual models outperform monolingual ones; the English TweetTopic training set is an order of magnitude larger than each target-language training set.

The paper lacks sufficient statistical rigor in many comparative claims: significance is only partially indicated in the table, and the methodology for significance testing is not described in the provided text.
The evaluation of prompted LLMs is not fully controlled or reproducible because proprietary models can change over time and prompt sensitivity is not systematically analyzed.
The paper does not deeply analyze label quality, per-topic support, or whether some topics are culturally or linguistically mismatched across languages.
There are presentation issues and some inconsistencies/typos that reduce clarity and polish.
methodological_flaws: The strongest scientific validity issue is the interpretation of cross-lingual superiority over monolingual training. Because TweetTopic has 11,267 English training examples while each target-language fold has only 720 training examples, the comparison does not isolate cross-lingual transfer from simple data-scale effects. The paper acknowledges this but still frames the result as evidence of strong cross-lingual capability; this conclusion is overstated without size-matched controls.

The label aggregation rule ('at least two annotators agree') is methodologically questionable for multi-label annotation with five annotators. This can admit labels supported by only a minority of annotators and likely inflates false positives/noise. Given low alpha scores, this weak consensus rule threatens empirical validity of both the benchmark and model comparisons.

The claim that weighted sampling by retweet count and follower count selects 'higher quality content' is not scientifically justified and introduces a popularity bias. Popularity is not equivalent to quality, and this choice may systematically skew the dataset toward celebrities, newsworthy users, or engagement-optimized content.

The preprocessing removes tweets with URLs and tweets with more than four emojis or mentions, which may disproportionately exclude important social-media genres and topic indicators. This may narrow the task distribution in a way not reflected in the paper's claims about realism.

The paper reports annotation agreement using Alpha, PA, and overlap, but does not clearly justify whether the chosen form of Krippendorff's alpha is appropriate for this multi-label setup, nor how it was computed. Without this detail, the reliability interpretation is harder to assess.

The few-shot setup selects five examples from the validation set to maximize topic coverage. If these examples are reused across evaluation in a way informed by the fold distribution, this may create a mild tuning bias; at minimum, the protocol should be specified more precisely.

The paper makes comparative claims about best models and underperformance of LLMs, but the benchmark mixes proprietary API models with fine-tuned open models under different cost, reproducibility, and optimization conditions. The conclusions are directionally useful but not fully apples-to-apples.

No error bars or variance estimates across folds are discussed in the main narrative, despite the small dataset size and likely instability of macro-F1 on rare labels. This weakens confidence in fine-grained ranking claims.
